passage:
Monday. Harsha stood in the ticket line at the suburban station when a man slid in three places ahead. Harsha said nothing. A woman with a heavy bag sighed, and a teenager stared at his phone. Harsha felt irritated but wasn’t sure it was worth a fight.
Thursday. The same man, Madhav, did it again. This time Harsha smiled and said, “Excuse me, the line starts back there. I’m running late too.”
Madhav blinked, grinned sheepishly and said, “Oh, sorry, didn’t notice.” He went to the back.
Saturday. Madhav stood at the end of the line and gave Harsha a small nod.

qa.q: What did Harsha say to Madhav on Thursday?
qa.a: Harsha said, “Excuse me, the line starts back there. I’m running late too.”

qa.q: Why did Harsha stay silent on Monday?
qa.a: Harsha felt irritated but was not sure it was worth a fight. Harsha weighed the tension against the small gain and let it pass that day.

qa.q: What made Harsha's comment on Thursday work?
qa.a: Harsha smiled, kept the tone light and shared that Harsha was late too. That let Madhav step back without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How might Madhav have felt when Harsha spoke to him?
qa.a: Madhav may have felt caught out and a bit embarrassed, since he grinned sheepishly. His nod on Saturday suggests he took the comment without resentment.

grounding: Shows a commuter observing someone jump a queue, weighing whether to speak, and finding a light polite comment works.

passage:
Vikas, sit, and I’ll tell you what I saw years ago. I’m Kavitha, and I was a junior clerk then, waiting for my train on a crowded platform.
A man finished his snack and dropped the wrapper on the track. Everyone saw it. Two men clicked their tongues, and one muttered about people these days.
The woman who ran the tea stall, stirring her pot, called out kindly, “Sir, the bin is right behind you. I can hold your tea.”
He went red, picked up the wrapper and dropped it in the bin. “Sorry, Amma,” he said, and took his tea.
I stood there with my scolding ready and never needed it.

qa.q: Where did the man drop the wrapper?
qa.a: The man dropped the wrapper on the track.

qa.q: How might the man who dropped the wrapper have felt when the tea stall woman spoke?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed, since he went red, but not attacked. Her kind tone gave him an easy way to fix it and say sorry.

qa.q: What choice did the tea stall woman make when others only clicked their tongues?
qa.a: She spoke to the man directly, pointed out the bin and offered to hold his tea. She gave him an easy step to take instead of a scolding.

qa.q: What might the two men who muttered have been feeling, compared with the tea stall woman?
qa.a: They seemed annoyed but did not want to speak to the man, so they grumbled among themselves, which changed nothing. The tea stall woman acted on it.

grounding: An elder recalls seeing a stall woman give a light, polite word to a litterer, showing how a friendly comment beats a scolding.
